lessons.title: Two independent questions: what starts and what ends a pulse?
lessons.physicalIntuition: A label may describe the timer while another describes the sensed state. Clocked peak-current PWM, valley-triggered one-shots, and current-programmed COT occupy different combinations of independent decisions.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Represent a controller as a tuple of start guard, end guard/timer, state feedback, frequency law, and outer-loop update. Use the tuple to classify architectures rather than forcing exclusive categories.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The taxonomy document expresses start and end rules as explicit tuples and supplies hybrid classification prompts. The current comparison plot does not construct arbitrary hybrid controllers interactively.
assumptions: taxonomy is descriptive, not a proof of performance
lessons.interaction: Control-taxonomy teach-back classifier using the documented start/end tuples
lessons.transferQuestion: Classify a controller whose voltage comparator starts a fixed on pulse but whose threshold is adjusted by average current error.

lessons.title: Matched-plant comparison
lessons.physicalIntuition: The same inductor/capacitor can respond differently because pulse decisions see different signals and delays. No mode is universally faster, quieter, or simpler independent of implementation.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Use matched normalized response templates to isolate qualitative damping, delay, noise, limit, and light-load tendencies. This is a heuristic comparison, not substitution of three controller state machines into one switched plant.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The current lab displays output-only, normalized damped-response proxies with scenario-specific metrics and visible exclusions. Controller waveforms, sensing, and compensation structures must be compared separately before making a design claim.
lessons.interaction: Control-mode comparison lab: startup, line step, load step, noise, and limit
lessons.transferQuestion: Which comparison conclusion reverses when comparator delay doubles, and why?

lessons.title: Behavioral-model complexity and failure modes
lessons.physicalIntuition: Each architecture moves complexity: explicit compensation, accurate current sensing, clean feedback ripple, scheduling, or mode logic. Omitting the hard part produces an unrealistically favorable model.
lessons.mathematicalDerivation: Trace each controller's decision variable sensitivity to noise, delay, and slope and identify its constrained timing inequalities.
lessons.modelingConsequence: The block-construction puzzle requires the architecture's essential sensor/timing blocks and highlights what is excluded.
assumptions: comparison scoped to disclosed decision rules
lessons.transferQuestion: Why would an ideal ripple source make a COT model look unfairly robust?
